tagline: Bilingual factual code knowledge, separated from whether a model can merely execute a snippet
overview: CodeSimpleQA tests a part of coding intelligence that execution benchmarks often blur: whether a model knows concrete facts about programming languages, frameworks, systems, algorithms, databases, and software practice. Its 1,498 human-curated question-answer pairs are split between 782 English and 716 Chinese items, cover more than 15 programming languages and 21 computer-science domains, and are checked against authoritative technical sources.

The paper reports separate domain-level F1 tables for Chinese and English. To keep the site comparison bilingual, TokenWave averages each model's English Avg. and Chinese Avg. values. The resulting Bilingual mean F1 is therefore a transparent derived score, not a third metric claimed by the authors; the original language-specific values remain traceable to Tables 3 and 4.
why: A model can produce executable code while still hallucinating an API contract, a language rule, or a systems fact. Those errors are especially costly in code review, debugging, migration, and technical support, where an authoritative-sounding false detail can steer an entire implementation. CodeSimpleQA isolates that factual layer and, by testing both English and Chinese, shows whether technical knowledge transfers across the two languages rather than hiding behind an English-only aggregate.
reading: GPT-5 leads the bilingual aggregation at 65.05, followed by o3 at 61.65 — a 3.40-point gap. GPT-5 Mini is another 6.00 points back at 55.65, while o4-mini and the two Claude Sonnet 4 variants occupy the next band from 53.30 to 51.90. The top-ten spread reaches 16.35 points, yet even the leader leaves almost 35 points of the scale unclaimed. On this benchmark, factual programming knowledge remains a distinct and visibly unsolved capability.
